question.prompt:
On Halloween \(31\) children walked into the principal’s office asking for candy. They can be classified into three types: Some always lie; some always tell the truth; and some alternately lie and tell the truth. The alternaters arbitrarily choose their first response, either a lie or the truth, but each subsequent statement has the opposite truth value from its predecessor. The principal asked everyone the same three questions in this order.

“Are you a truth-teller?” The principal gave a piece of candy to each of the \(22\) children who answered yes.

“Are you an alternater?” The principal gave a piece of candy to each of the \(15\) children who answered yes.

“Are you a liar?” The principal gave a piece of candy to each of the \(9\) children who answered yes.

How many pieces of candy in all did the principal give to the children who always tell the truth?

solutions.explanation:
Compare the first two questions. The only children who say yes to the first but not the second are the truth-tellers.

To see why, follow each type. A truth-teller answers yes, then no. A liar answers yes to both: the truthful answers would be no to both. An alternater who lies first says yes to the first question and then truthfully says yes to the second. An alternater who tells the truth first says no, then falsely says no.

Thus the \(22\) yes answers to the first question consist of all \(15\) children who say yes to the second, plus the truth-tellers. There are \(22-15=7\) truth-tellers. Each says no to the third question, so each receives just one piece of candy.

The requested total is \(\boxed{7}\), choice A. Comparing answer patterns can eliminate unknown groups without finding every group's size.
solutions.title: Compare yes-answer patterns for the first two questions.
